notes.meaning: Jesus and His followers came near to Jerusalem, stopping by the Mount of Olives near Bethphage and Bethany. He chose two of His disciples and sent them ahead on a special task. Jesus was not hiding from the leaders who hated Him, but was openly moving toward His coming death. He directed every detail with care to fulfill God's plan.

Jesus told the disciples to enter the village ahead, where they would immediately find a young donkey tied up. No person had ever ridden this animal before. By riding an unbroken colt, Jesus showed His humble spirit as a king of peace, as well as His mastery over nature.

Jesus knew someone might question why the disciples were taking the animal. He instructed them to say that the Lord had need of it and would return it promptly. Even in His poverty, the Lord showed that He has the right to use whatever belongs to His people.

The two disciples went and found the young colt tied by an outside doorway in the street, exactly as Jesus had said. When local bystanders asked what they were doing, the disciples repeated the words Jesus gave them. Hearing that the Master needed the animal, the people willingly let them lead it away.

The disciples brought the young donkey to Jesus and placed their outer coats across its back to serve as a saddle. Jesus then sat upon the colt to make His entry into the city. This simple animal carried the King of glory in meekness rather than worldly pride.

Crowds of pilgrims welcomed Jesus by laying their coats down on the dusty road before Him. Others cut leafy branches and rushes from the surrounding fields and spread them in His path. This was an ancient way of honoring a ruler and giving Him a royal reception.

The people marching in front and behind cried out words of praise from the Psalms. They shouted 'Hosanna', which means 'Save now, please', and blessed the one coming as God's chosen messenger. They rejoiced that the promised kingdom of David was finally arriving in their midst.

Jesus entered Jerusalem and walked straight into the temple courts, which were the open areas surrounding God's holy house. He silently inspected everything taking place there, observing how the worship was being conducted. Because it was already late in the day, He left the city to spend the night with His twelve apostles in Bethany.

The next morning, as Jesus and His disciples walked back toward Jerusalem from Bethany, He felt genuine physical hunger. This shows that the Lord truly shared our human nature and felt ordinary bodily needs. His desire for food set the stage for an important spiritual lesson.

Jesus spotted a fig tree full of green leaves in the distance and walked over to see if it held any early fruit. He found nothing on it but leaves, because the normal time for gathering ripe figs had not yet arrived. On fig trees, the fruit usually appears along with or before the leaves, so the leafy display gave a false promise of food.

differ.view: Charles Spurgeon applied the phrase about the season not yet arriving to God's chosen people who are not yet converted, but who will certainly be changed when God's timing and grace arrive.
John Wesley suggested the phrase could simply mean it was a poor year for figs, or that the harvest season had not arrived so the tree should not have already been stripped of its fruit.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching often treats the note about the season as theological rather than agricultural, viewing the cursed tree as a living symbol that the era of old temple worship had run its course.

notes.meaning: Jesus spoke directly to the tree and declared that no one would ever eat fruit from it again. His disciples listened carefully and remembered what He had commanded. The curse was not an act of petty anger, but a living parable showing the coming judgment on religious hypocrisy.

Upon reaching the temple, Jesus began driving out the merchants and shoppers who had turned the sacred area into a marketplace. He pushed over the money tables and the benches belonging to men selling doves for sacrifices. He acted with divine authority to cleanse His Father's house from dishonest trade.

Jesus stopped people from carrying everyday equipment, trade goods, and vessels through the temple courts. Many people had been using the sacred grounds as a shortcut between the city and the Mount of Olives. He demanded that proper reverence and respect be restored to the place dedicated to God.

Jesus reminded the people that Scripture calls God's house a place of prayer for all nations. The leaders had crowded out Gentile worshippers and allowed greedy traders to turn the outer court into a hideout for thieves. True worship must be open to everyone and kept free from selfish greed.

The leading priests and teachers of the law heard about His actions and began plotting a way to kill Him. They were terrified of His influence because the ordinary crowds were completely amazed by His powerful teaching. The leaders cared more about protecting their own status than hearing God's truth.

When darkness began to fall, Jesus and His disciples quietly left Jerusalem. He stayed outside the city walls at night to avoid unnecessary riots or premature arrest before His appointed time. Bethany provided a safe retreat where He could rest.

Passing along the road the following morning, the disciples noticed the fig tree they had seen the day before. It was completely dried up and dead, all the way down to its roots. This sudden death showed that the Lord's sentence of judgment was total and final.

Peter recalled what Jesus had said the day before and pointed out that the cursed tree was entirely withered. He was stunned by how swiftly the tree had died under the Master's spoken word. Jesus used Peter's surprise to turn their minds toward spiritual trust.

Jesus answered Peter by urging the disciples to put their complete faith in God. He wanted them to focus their hearts on God's almighty power rather than merely being surprised by a withered tree. True faith leans entirely upon God, who can do all things with absolute ease.

differ.view: Some older Holiness writers distinguished ordinary faith in God for forgiveness from the 'faith of God', which they saw as a higher, perfect faith received at entire sanctification.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The traditional Catholic Douay-Rheims version translates the phrase literally as 'Have the faith of God.'

notes.meaning: Jesus told them that whoever commands a mountain to be thrown into the sea, without doubting in his heart, will see it done. He was using a familiar Jewish picture of moving a mountain to describe overcoming seemingly impossible barriers. When God directs our prayers, no spiritual obstacle can stand against genuine trust in Him.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Word of Faith teachers use this verse to claim that human words have supernatural creative force, so believers can bring whatever they speak into existence.

notes.meaning: Jesus taught that when we pray, we should believe that God will grant what we request, and it will be given. This promise calls believers to ask with earnest confidence, resting on God's revealed character and promises. It is an invitation to rely wholeheartedly on His goodness whenever we pray.

differ.view: Reformed teachers stress that this promise must align with God's sovereign will and warn that treating it as a formula to demand whatever one wants distorts genuine biblical prayer.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Prosperity preachers teach that this verse guarantees Christians will receive any earthly blessing or health they request if they only picture and claim it with enough faith.

notes.meaning: Jesus added that whenever we stand to pray, we must forgive anyone who has wronged us. A bitter, unforgiving heart blocks our fellowship with God and hinders our prayers. If we expect our heavenly Father to forgive our daily sins, we must show that same mercy to others.

This verse warns that if we refuse to forgive those who hurt us, our Father in heaven will not forgive our wrongdoing. Refusing to forgive shows that our hearts do not truly understand or value God's grace. Daily pardon from God requires a spirit that extends kindness to our neighbors.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Textual scholars note that the earliest Greek manuscripts do not contain this verse, suggesting it was added by later copyists from the parallel teaching in Matthew 6:15.

notes.meaning: Jesus returned to Jerusalem and walked among the colonnades of the temple courts, teaching the crowds. A delegation of chief priests, scribes, and Jewish elders approached Him to stage a formal challenge. These leaders formed the ruling council and wanted to stop His growing influence.

The leaders demanded to know what right Jesus had to cleanse the temple and teach as He did, and who had granted Him such power. Because they had not licensed Him, they hoped to show the crowd that He was acting illegally. They sought to trap Him into saying something they could use to condemn Him.

Jesus replied by setting a fair condition before answering their challenge. He told them He would ask a single question first, and if they answered it honestly, He would tell them by what authority He acted. His wise counter-question tested whether they truly cared about the truth.

Jesus asked them whether John's baptism was authorized by God in heaven or was merely an invention of human origin. He pressed them firmly for a direct answer. Because John had pointed directly to Jesus, their view of John would reveal their real attitude toward Him.

The rulers stepped aside to whisper among themselves about how to answer. If they admitted that John was sent by God, Jesus would ask why they refused to believe John's message. But if they claimed John was just an ordinary man, they were terrified the crowd would turn on them, since the people firmly believed John was a genuine prophet.

Trapped by their own dishonesty, the leaders claimed they did not know where John's authority came from. Jesus told them that He would not tell them His authority either. Because they willfully closed their eyes to God's obvious truth, they did not deserve any further explanation.
